1.stem: [Academic Talk — Seismology] According to the professor, what did the survey of the surviving seismograms show about the collection?

options.A: Roughly half the sheets survive, with the losses concentrated in the years the network changed hands
options.B: The record is thin before 1915, since stations then reused sheets that showed no visible events
options.C: Sheets from three stations were interfiled decades ago, and reattributing them has taken most of the project's first year
options.D: The sheets survive nearly complete, but many were trimmed for framing and lost their margins with the time marks

2.stem: [Academic Talk — Papyrology] What did the professor say the fiber analysis established about the pieces in the lot?

options.A: A dozen pieces entered in the register as papyrus are parchment, a slip nobody has caught since
options.B: The sheets fall into two manufacturing qualities, mixed indifferently across the documentary and literary pieces
options.C: Repairs made in antiquity used strips from a discarded letter, itself now the oldest text in the lot
options.D: Several literary pieces were written on reused account rolls, with the accounts still legible on the back

3.stem: [Academic Talk — Dance History] What did the professor say the study of the roll's notation established about how much of the dance it records?

options.A: It lays out the floor patterns fully, while the steps themselves are left to a few conventional signs
options.B: It records the corps in detail and reduces the soloists' variations to a line of description each
options.C: It gives the mime scenes at the same length as the dancing, where later notations drop them
options.D: It carries two numbers complete and no more than the opening figures for the rest

4.stem: [Academic Talk — Entomology] What is the professor's assessment of the claim that the beetle disappeared from the coastal meadows early in the twentieth century?

options.A: He suspects the species moved into the drained margins nearby, where nobody thought to sweep
options.B: He argues the apparent disappearance tracks where collectors went, not where the beetle lived
options.C: He thinks the older records rest on misidentified relatives, so there is no disappearance to explain
options.D: He is persuaded, noting that later collectors worked the same meadows hard and came back without it

5.stem: [Academic Talk — Epigraphy] Why does the professor bring up the parsonage at Kolgama?

options.A: Its glebe wall was rebuilt with fragments from two of the stones, which is how those pieces survived
options.B: Its successive pastors kept the visitation books in which the stones are first mentioned
options.C: Its attic held the bundle of paper squeezes, found again when the roof was renewed in the 1960s
options.D: The professor once catalogued its library, an aside about how he came to the material in the first place

6.stem: [Academic Talk — Garden History] Why does the professor bring up the head gardener Tiidema's letter-book?

options.A: It shows he trained at Kaldevere from boyhood, against the story that he was hired from abroad
options.B: Its blotting pages preserve impressions of letters sent, including several the family later destroyed
options.C: His weekly letters to the absent family amount to a garden diary nobody meant to keep
options.D: It records his running quarrel with a neighboring estate's gardener, the professor's favorite thread in the archive

7.stem: [Academic Talk — Historical Demography] What does the professor imply the project will take up next?

options.A: Extending the same reading to the neighboring parishes whose registers survive in fair shape
options.B: Linking the register families to the manor's rent rolls to follow survivors across the crisis
options.C: Bringing in the grain price series to test how the crisis lines up with the harvests
options.D: Reconstituting a sample of households in full, a slower method she has argued the material can support

8.stem: [Academic Talk — Dance History] What does the professor imply the research group will do with the roll next?

options.A: Stage a reconstruction of one suite with students, treating the performance itself as a test of the notation
options.B: Compare its figures against provincial ballroom manuals to see how far the stage dances circulated
options.C: Take the roll to the conservation lab and have its rubbed passages read under raking light
options.D: Set the notation beside the orchestral parts in the theater library to fix the numbers' order

9.stem: [Academic Talk — Acoustics] What is the professor's judgment on the hall's reputation for extraordinary sound?

options.A: She thinks the reputation grew after the demolition, fed by memoir writers mourning the building
options.B: She credits it, and points to measured values that a modern designer would still envy
options.C: She reads the fame as a period taste for long reverberation that later audiences stopped prizing
options.D: She ties the fame to the orchestra in residence, whose sound traveled with it on tour

10.stem: [Academic Talk — Entomology] What did the professor say the study of the handwriting on the labels revealed?

options.A: Two assistants wrote most of the labels, and their abbreviations for the coastal sites differ
options.B: The hand on the oldest labels matches Sarvela's schoolmaster, pushing the collection's start a generation earlier
options.C: Some labels were rewritten during a 1930s re-curation, with the original spellings modernized
options.D: The localities were inked over earlier pencil, showing the labels were finished in two sittings

11.stem: [Academic Talk — Limnology] Why does the professor mention the minute-books of the fishermen's association?

options.A: Their complaints about net fouling give dated sightings of the weed beds the surveys missed
options.B: They show the catch was weighed at the landing for decades, a series long enough to be worth mining
options.C: An argument written up in them preserves where the association believed the springs entered the lake
options.D: They record the association paying Virkland's boatman, which fixes the survey seasons the notebooks leave vague

12.stem: [Academic Talk — Limnology] What did the professor say the comparison of Virkland's transparency readings with the modern series showed?

options.A: His figures run consistently deeper, by about the margin his larger disk and calm-day habits would produce
options.B: The comparison holds on the open lake but breaks down in the bays, which he visited twice a season
options.C: His numbers scatter too widely to carry a trend, though the notebooks explain the scatter honestly
options.D: The two series agree closely once his summer readings are set against modern ones from the same weeks

13.stem: [Academic Talk — Acoustics] What does the professor imply the group plans to do next?

options.A: Mount an exhibition pairing the laboratory's instruments with photographs showing the hall in use
options.B: Measure the architect's surviving smaller hall in a nearby town as a stand-in for the lost one
options.C: Comb the local press for what listeners said about the hall when it was new
options.D: Rebuild a section of the vanished wall at full scale and measure how much sound it absorbs

14.stem: [Academic Talk — Entomology] What does the professor suggest the museum team will do next with the Sarvela collection?

options.A: Screen the older series for the mites that ride on the beetles, a fauna nobody has examined
options.B: Send fragments of selected specimens for DNA work, starting with the series whose localities are secure
options.C: Trace the duplicates that were traded to other museums and reunite the data, if not the specimens
options.D: Re-pin the material onto archival mounts, photographing each label before it is moved

15.stem: [Academic Talk — Garden History] What did the professor say the nursery invoices revealed?

options.A: Most stock came from the estate's own nursery, with outside orders reserved for novelties
options.B: The orders date the water garden some thirty years later than the guidebooks have it
options.C: Substitutions were constant, with the nursery sending hardier kinds than the ones ordered
options.D: The invoices are addressed to the countess, putting the purchasing in her hands rather than the steward's

16.stem: [Academic Talk — Epigraphy] What did the professor say the comparison of Vaissalu's drawings with the surviving stones showed?

options.A: He recorded the texts accurately but placed three stones at the wrong churchyards
options.B: Several drawings copy an earlier antiquarian's sketches rather than the stones, repeating that man's misreadings
options.C: Where the surface had flaked, he supplied plausible letters of his own without marking them as guesses
options.D: The letterforms are rendered faithfully, though the drawings compress the spacing between lines to fit his page

17.stem: [Academic Talk — Epigraphy] What is the professor's position on the argument that the stones were carved long after the dates they bear?

options.A: He narrows it, holding that a single carver's late pieces created the impression for the whole group
options.B: He rejects it, arguing the weathering on the carved faces needs far longer than the argument allows
options.C: He grants the late carving, resting the case on memorial formulas that echo printed models issued much later
options.D: He accepts it for the group as a whole, persuaded by letter shapes that belong to a later century

18.stem: [Academic Talk — Papyrology] What does the professor imply the editors will do next?

options.A: Seek joins with a collection in another city that bought from the same source in the same season
options.B: Bring out the documentary texts first, since the literary fragments will take years to piece together
options.C: Build a concordance of the hands across the lot, to see how many scribes are represented
options.D: Image the cartonnage without dismantling it, and read what they can from the scans

19.stem: [Academic Talk — Seismology] Why does the professor bring up the logbook kept at the Luhemaa station?

options.A: It preserves the observer's own felt account, written within an hour, which no newspaper carried
options.B: It shows the station kept running for a decade longer than the official history states
options.C: Its weather entries let the team rule out storm surf as the source of a puzzling background signal
options.D: An entry in it led the team to a crate of records believed discarded in the 1950s

20.stem: [Academic Talk — Acoustics] What did the professor say the laboratory notebooks showed about how the Kuivalinn hall was measured?

options.A: The figures entered are averages, with the single readings kept on cards that survive separately
options.B: Readings were taken with the seats filled by workers from a nearby factory, given the afternoon off for it
options.C: Rebasmaa repeated the series after a renovation, and both campaigns are written up in the same book
options.D: The measurements used pistol shots from the stage, logged position by position across two evenings

21.stem: [Academic Talk — Dance History] Why does the professor mention the customs stamp on the roll's wrapper?

options.A: It fixes a border crossing that puts the roll in the company's baggage on its final tour
options.B: It shows the roll entered the country from the south, not with the company returning from the west
options.C: It shows the wrapper is reused freight paper, so the address on it has misled earlier researchers
options.D: It dates the wrapper decades after the roll, showing the two traveled separately before being joined

22.stem: [Academic Talk — Papyrology] Why does the professor bring up the day-book kept by the dealer Pellamaa?

options.A: Its running numbers show the lot was renumbered at sale, which explains a long-standing confusion in the catalogues
options.B: Its blank stretches match the years the excavation permits were suspended, which the trade felt at once
options.C: Its entries pace out the sales month by month, showing how slowly material of this kind moved
options.D: It names a silent partner in the trade whose own papers may still be in family hands

23.stem: [Academic Talk — Historical Demography] According to the professor, what did the close study of the crisis entries themselves show?

options.A: Each entry names who brought word of the death, and for long stretches it was one household
options.B: Stillbirths and infants are kept in a separate list at the back, which the printed abstracts pass over
options.C: A cause is entered for the first year of the crisis and then dropped, the column left blank
options.D: Burials were entered several days at a time, so their day-level dating is the historians' and not the parish's

24.stem: [Academic Talk — Garden History] What is the professor's central claim about the relationship between the garden as planted and the drawings in the estate archive?

options.A: The drawings governed the walled gardens, while the park beyond grew by improvisation season to season
options.B: The main drawing guided the first campaign closely, and was set aside within a decade as taste turned
options.C: The showpiece drawing tidies the beds into a symmetry the planting on the ground did not follow
options.D: The planted garden braided two rival drawings, taking its structure from one and its planting from the other

25.stem: [Academic Talk — Acoustics] What is the professor's central point about what the surviving recordings made in the hall can establish?

options.A: Heard against studio discs by the same players, they isolate what the room added to the sound
options.B: They document the placement of the musicians more than the room, since the horn favored whoever faced it
options.C: Digitally cleaned, they can anchor a computed model of the hall that no drawing on its own could support
options.D: They tell us mostly about performing style, because the room's contribution sits below what the discs preserve

26.stem: [Academic Talk — Papyrology] What is the professor's central claim about where the Aravik lot came from?

options.A: Most of it had passed through an earlier collection, dispersed a generation before, whose marks survive on the frames
options.B: It came out of a town rubbish mound worked over several winters, not from tombs as the sale notice claimed
options.C: Pellamaa assembled it from several finds, matching pieces by look to make a more salable whole
options.D: It was found as one group in a sealed jar, the pieces' shared damp stain still recording how they were stacked

27.stem: [Academic Talk — Epigraphy] What does the professor suggest the project will do about the stones that have not been located?

options.A: Leave them out of the corpus volume and treat them in a separate article
options.B: Ask the national radio to run an appeal, a method that has turned up carved stones before
options.C: Publish them from Vaissalu's drawings alone, with the readings flagged as unverified
options.D: Circulate a handlist to county museums, on the chance some sit unrecognized in storerooms

28.stem: [Academic Talk — Seismology] What is the professor's view of the proposal linking the 1907 earthquake to the Kolmsaare fault?

options.A: He prefers a rival structure to the north, which he argues fits the coastal uplift better
options.B: He credits the link, but reads the fault as an inherited weakness re-used rather than a young structure
options.C: He finds it persuasive, chiefly because the aftershocks line up along the structure's mapped trend
options.D: He doubts any mapped fault is needed, reading the region's earthquakes as scattered through old, healed crust

29.stem: [Academic Talk — Historical Demography] Why does the professor mention the rebinding the volumes underwent in the 1880s?

options.A: The bill for the work survives and names which volumes there were, showing one has since gone missing
options.B: It stamped an archive's crest on the covers, the clue that let the books' wanderings be traced
options.C: The binder trimmed the margins, taking off annotations that an earlier antiquarian had luckily transcribed
options.D: A few leaves from the next parish upriver were bound in by mistake, a mix-up caught in the 1930s

30.stem: [Academic Talk — Entomology] Why does the professor bring up the 1904 auction catalogue?

options.A: A pencil note in one copy identifies the buyer whose heirs later gave the material to the museum
options.B: The prices it records show how little value insect material had then, which explains the careless storage
options.C: It lists a cabinet that has not been seen since, which the professor calls the collection's real loss
options.D: Its lot descriptions let the team match unlabeled boxes to the collections they came from

31.stem: [Academic Talk — Limnology] What does the professor imply the team will do when fieldwork resumes at Soorna?

options.A: Sample the smaller lakes on the same moraine, to see whether Soorna's story is its own or the district's
options.B: Recover the survey's sunken marker buoys, whose positions anchor the old depth grid
options.C: Bring the landowners into the sampling rounds, trading access for a say in the program
options.D: Instrument the outflow through a winter, the season the old surveys left untouched

32.stem: [Academic Talk — Garden History] What is the professor's position on the attribution of the Kaldevere garden to Nurmsaar?

options.A: She reassigns the work to his pupil, whose planting lists elsewhere match Kaldevere's beds closely
options.B: She upholds the design but doubts he came, arguing the plans traveled by post and were adapted on site
options.C: She reads the garden as the family's own project, dressed with the designer's name a generation later
options.D: She upholds it, resting her case on a payment the estate books enter for his summer visit

33.stem: [Academic Talk — Dance History] What is the professor's position on the claim that the roll records the ballet as it was first staged?

options.A: She reads it as a teaching document, setting down what dancers were drilled on rather than any staging given
options.B: She endorses the claim, finding in the ensemble figures the crowded groupings the first reviews complained of
options.C: She endorses it for the figures, though she takes the entrances to have been redrawn for a later season
options.D: She reads the roll as a record of the revival, with the ensemble numbers already thinned

34.stem: [Academic Talk — Historical Demography] What is the professor's central claim about what the Turvaste registers show for the crisis years?

options.A: Deaths were concentrated among recent arrivals, while long-settled families came through comparatively lightly
options.B: The parish lost people mainly to departure, with households leaving for the towns rather than dying
options.C: Losses fell hardest on the outlying hamlets, while the church village itself was less touched
options.D: The crisis came in two waves a year apart, and the second was the heavier one

35.stem: [Academic Talk — Seismology] What is the professor's central claim about what the re-analysis changed in the picture of the 1907 earthquake?

options.A: The source lay well out under the sea, not beneath the coastal parish the catalogues name
options.B: What was catalogued as one shock was two ruptures minutes apart, blended together in contemporary accounts
options.C: The magnitude comes down appreciably once the old instruments' exaggerated response is taken into account
options.D: The damage pattern owed more to ground conditions in the river towns than to the size of the event

36.stem: [Academic Talk — Limnology] How does the professor respond to Kivrand's argument that the darkening of Soorna's water began centuries before the first surveys?

options.A: He rejects it, arguing the signals Kivrand relies on move whenever a lake's level shifts, whatever the water's color
options.B: He endorses it, and takes the pollen and charcoal work to push the beginning further back still
options.C: He accepts an early start but dates it later than Kivrand does, closer to the received view
options.D: He reads the darkening as periodic rather than a single onset, returning with the wetter centuries
